blindSummary:
This is a serious-risk destination for trans visitors. Same-sex activity is criminalised (up to 1 year, or more under aggravating provisions), and because there is no legal gender recognition, trans people are legally treated as their birth sex — meaning a trans person's ordinary relationships can be prosecuted as same-sex conduct. A 2024 stakeholder report to the UN periodic review documents discrimination, violence, and absence of police protection, with trans women and queer women particularly at risk, plus a growing organised anti-LGBTQ+ campaign inside the country.

Documented trans-specific enforcement is thinner than in some neighbouring countries — the country's LGBTQ+ community (which uses a locally coined self-identifier) is deeply underground, and reporting is sparse — but the legal structure (criminalisation plus the absence of any legal-gender-recognition catch-all), hostile campaigning, and absence of any protection keep the practical risk severe. Digital surveillance and blackmail vulnerability are noted in the periodic-review reporting.
blindOutOfScope: Same-sex criminalisation captures trans people via birth-sex legal status — a direct, not situational, mechanism.
blindSourceSummaries: Stakeholder submission to this country's UN periodic review (47th session): same-sex activity criminalised, leaving LGBTQ+ people at serious risk of harm and systematic exclusion; discrimination, violence, lack of police protection and stigma in services; no legal gender change - trans men are legally women and trans women legally men, so trans people in different-gender relationships can fall foul of the same-sex conduct law.

Stakeholder periodic-review report by an international human-rights NGO and its local partner organisation (April 2024) on SOGIE in this country: documents discrimination, violence, and lack of protection; notes transgender people are particularly at risk given the criminalisation framework.
A global LGBT-barometer survey's country profile for this country: composite LGBT-rights perception scores including its transgender-rights index.
A foreign government's 2008 human-rights report on this country (archived): documents the criminalisation of same-sex conduct and societal stigma - baseline country-of-origin information.

A foreign government's 2011 human-rights report on this country (archived): documents arrests of opposition figures, civil-society-law restrictions, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal discrimination.

A foreign government's 2010 human-rights report on this country: documents anti-terrorism prosecutions, civil-society-law restrictions, torture, harsh prisons - general context with the LGBT section noting criminalisation.

Master's thesis (2009) at a foreign university on homosexuality in this country - analyses the construction of homosexuality in relation to gender and feminism; male homosexuality criminalised (up to 3 years); media and elites create homophobia in discourse; the dominant religious institution effectively campaigns hatred; female homosexuality simply overlooked; attitudes shifting under globalisation.
blindTangential: Same-sex criminalisation (up to 1 year, more under aggravation) — because there is no legal gender recognition, a trans person's relationships are legally same-sex; a direct mechanism, not merely climate.
